claim: Humans perform saccadic eye movements two to three times per second.
source: Humans perform saccadic eye movements two to three times per second.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact about human eye movement behavior.

claim: The nervous system strongly suppresses sensory feedback for extended periods of time during saccades in comparison to movement time.
source: When doing so, the nervous system strongly suppresses sensory feedback for extended periods of time in comparison to movement time.
evidence: This is presented as an established characteristic of saccadic suppression.

claim: A Bayesian estimator should reduce the weight of sensory information around the time of saccades as a result of signal dependent noise and sensorimotor delays.
source: More precisely, we show theoretically that a Bayesian estimator should reduce the weight of sensory information around the time of saccades, as a result of signal dependent noise and of sensorimotor delays.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction derived from the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: The reduction in sensory weight predicted by the Bayesian estimator parallels the behavioral suppression occurring prior to and during saccades.
source: Such reduction parallels the behavioral suppression occurring prior to and during saccades, and the reduction in neural responses to visual stimuli observed across the visual hierarchy.
evidence: This is a comparison between the model prediction and known behavioral phenomena.

claim: There is a reduction in neural responses to visual stimuli across the visual hierarchy during saccades.
source: Such reduction parallels the behavioral suppression occurring prior to and during saccades, and the reduction in neural responses to visual stimuli observed across the visual hierarchy.
evidence: This refers to established neurophysiological observations.

claim: Saccadic suppression originates from efficient sensorimotor processing.
source: We suggest that saccadic suppression originates from efficient sensorimotor processing, indicating that the brain shares neural resources for perception and control.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their theoretical model.

claim: The brain shares neural resources for perception and control.
source: We suggest that saccadic suppression originates from efficient sensorimotor processing, indicating that the brain shares neural resources for perception and control.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the theoretical model results.

claim: People skillfully combine acquired knowledge and sensory feedback using Bayesian statistics.
source: People skillfully combine acquired knowledge, and sensory feedback, a combination that is typically modeled using Bayesian statistics (Körding, 2007; Angelaki et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The Bayesian framework effectively captures behavior in perceptual decision-making tasks.
source: This framework effectively captures behavior in numerous tasks broadly corresponding to perceptual decision-making (Ernst and Banks, 2002; van Beers et al., 1999; Fetsch et al., 2011; Drugowitsch et al., 2014; Acuna et al., 2015), or online movement control (Wolpert et al., 1995; Körding and Wolpert, 2004; Izawa and Shadmehr, 2008; Crevecoeur et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The Bayesian framework effectively captures behavior in online movement control tasks.
source: This framework effectively captures behavior in numerous tasks broadly corresponding to perceptual decision-making (Ernst and Banks, 2002; van Beers et al., 1999; Fetsch et al., 2011; Drugowitsch et al., 2014; Acuna et al., 2015), or online movement control (Wolpert et al., 1995; Körding and Wolpert, 2004; Izawa and Shadmehr, 2008; Crevecoeur et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Perceptual decision-making and sensorimotor control cannot really be dissociated in the real world.
source: Although perceptual decision-making and sensorimotor control are often considered different phenomena, they cannot really be dissociated in the real world – we need to use the same brain for movement and perception (Cisek, 2012; Wolpert and Landy, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents a conceptual argument.

claim: Visual acuity is reduced around the time of a saccade.
source: A salient case of crosstalk between perception and sensorimotor behavior is saccadic suppression: visual acuity is reduced around the time of a saccade.
evidence: This is a well-established behavioral phenomenon.

claim: Saccadic suppression is often assumed to maintain stable perception of our surroundings.
source: It is often assumed that this mechanism maintains stable perception of our surroundings (Wurtz, 2008).
evidence: This is a commonly held view supported by citation.

claim: Saccadic suppression is controlled centrally.
source: Indeed, previous work has shown that saccadic suppression is controlled centrally, and typically lasts for >100 ms even for saccadic movements of ~50 ms (Ibbotson and Krekelberg, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Saccadic suppression typically lasts for >100 ms even for saccadic movements of ~50 ms.
source: Indeed, previous work has shown that saccadic suppression is controlled centrally, and typically lasts for >100 ms even for saccadic movements of ~50 ms (Ibbotson and Krekelberg, 2011).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from previous research.

claim: Simulating the displacement of the retinal image without a saccade does not elicit similar suppression as during real saccades.
source: Furthermore, simulating the displacement of the retinal image without a saccade does not elicit similar suppression as during real saccades (Diamond et al., 2000; Thiele et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from previous studies.

claim: The reduction of visual acuity during saccades selectively impacts the magnocellular pathway.
source: As well, the reduction of visual acuity was reported to selectively impact the magnocellular pathway (Burr et al., 1994), although motion detection is still active (Castet and Masson, 2000).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from previous research.

claim: Motion detection is still active during saccades.
source: As well, the reduction of visual acuity was reported to selectively impact the magnocellular pathway (Burr et al., 1994), although motion detection is still active (Castet and Masson, 2000).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from previous research.

claim: Uncertainty about the instantaneous state of the eye should increase with motor commands as a result of signal-dependent noise and sensorimotor delays.
source: Indeed, our model shows that uncertainty about the instantaneous state of the eye should increase with motor commands as a result of signal-dependent noise and of sensorimotor delays, making delayed sensory information less reliable around the time of movement.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: Increased uncertainty makes delayed sensory information less reliable around the time of movement.
source: Indeed, our model shows that uncertainty about the instantaneous state of the eye should increase with motor commands as a result of signal-dependent noise and of sensorimotor delays, making delayed sensory information less reliable around the time of movement.
evidence: This is a logical consequence derived from the model.

claim: In an optimal estimation framework, increased uncertainty gives lower weights to sensory inputs when we move.
source: In an optimal estimation framework, this gives lower weights to sensory inputs when we move.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on optimal estimation principles.

claim: Saccades are monitored online through the corollary discharge.
source: First, the nature of the representation matters: although saccades are often simplistically viewed as ballistic (or open-loop) movements, these movements are monitored online through the corollary discharge (Van Gisbergen et al., 1981; West et al., 2009; Goossens and Van Opstal, 2000; Xu-Wilson et al., 2011; Sommer and Wurtz, 2008; Optican, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: There is no peripheral interruption of sensory inflow during saccades.
source: There is no peripheral interruption of sensory inflow, and information about specific spatiotemporal frequency or color is still good (Burr et al., 1994; Burr and Morrone, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Information about specific spatiotemporal frequency or color is still good during saccades.
source: There is no peripheral interruption of sensory inflow, and information about specific spatiotemporal frequency or color is still good (Burr et al., 1994; Burr and Morrone, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Target jumps during long saccades can influence movement.
source: Moreover, target jumps during long saccades can influence movement (Gaveau et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from previous research.

claim: The model reproduces stereotyped, step-like trajectories like those found during real saccades.
source: The model reproduces stereotyped, step-like trajectories (Figure 1b, top), like those found during real saccades.
evidence: This is a comparison between model output and known behavioral data, with reference to Figure 1b.

claim: The model produces a pattern of control with a wide agonist burst followed by a short, sharp antagonistic inflection.
source: Moreover, the associated commands provide a typically wide agonist burst, followed by a short, sharp antagonistic inflection, which stabilizes the eye at the target (Figure 1b, bottom).
evidence: This is a description of the model output shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The pattern of control produced by the model is compatible with the pattern of burst neurons that generate saccades.
source: This pattern of control, shaped by the fast time constants of the oculomotor plant, is compatible with the pattern of burst neurons that generate saccades (Van Gisbergen et al., 1981).
evidence: This is a comparison between model output and known neurophysiological data, supported by citation.

claim: The model reproduces typical responses to changes in target velocity occurring with or without initial target jump.
source: The model reproduces typical responses to changes in target velocity, occurring with or without initial target jump (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a description of model behavior shown in Figure 1c.

claim: When the target starts moving, position error accumulates over the delay interval, requiring a rapid compensatory movement to catch up with the target.
source: When the target starts moving (velocity jump), position error accumulates over the delay interval, which in turn requires a rapid compensatory movement to catch up with the target (Figure 1b, light blue).
evidence: This is an explanation of model behavior with reference to Figure 1b.

claim: The catch-up saccade naturally falls out of the simultaneous correction for errors both in position and velocity.
source: Although the controller was not explicitly designed to model the interaction between saccades and pursuit, the catch-up saccade in Figure 1b naturally falls out of the simultaneous correction for errors both in position and velocity.
evidence: This is an explanation of emergent model behavior.

claim: When the target jumps backwards at the onset of the velocity jump, the eye starts moving smoothly and there is no catch-up saccade.
source: In contrast, when the target jumps backwards at the onset of the velocity jump (Figure 1c, dark blue), the eye starts moving smoothly and there is no catch-up saccade (Rashbass, 1961).
evidence: This is a description of model behavior with reference to Figure 1c and citation to known experimental result.

claim: Muscles produce signal dependent noise; the stronger the muscles pull, the more noisy the state.
source: Our muscles produce signal dependent noise; the stronger the muscles pull, the more noisy the state.
evidence: This is a known property of motor control systems.

claim: The phasic activity associated with the agonist burst induces a peak in the variance of the control signal.
source: The phasic activity associated with the agonist burst induces a peak in the variance of the control signal (Figure 2a, solid).
evidence: This is shown in the model simulation data in Figure 2a.

claim: Because of the delay, there is no way for the nervous system to directly subtract or filter out motor noise.
source: Thus motor commands produce instantaneous noise, and because of the delay, there is no way for the nervous system to directly subtract or filter out this noise.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the consequences of sensorimotor delays.

claim: Moving the eye effectively induces visual uncertainty, which can only go back to baseline after the end of muscle activation.
source: In other words, moving the eye effectively induces visual uncertainty, which can only go back to baseline after the end of muscle activation.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the model.

claim: The period of suppression predicted by the model is long because the high variance period includes the movement time in addition to the delay.
source: The period of suppression predicted by the model is long because the high variance period includes the movement time in addition to the delay (gray rectangle in Figure 2c).
evidence: This is an explanation of model predictions with reference to Figure 2c.

claim: The model predicts that the onset of saccadic suppression should precede movement onset by a time interval equal to the delay, which was fixed to 100 ms in the model.
source: The model predicts that the onset of saccadic suppression should precede movement onset by a time interval equal to the delay, which was fixed to 100 ms in the model (see Materials and methods), although previous work suggested that it could be shorter (Gaveau et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative prediction from the model.

claim: Processing times in the retina approach ~50 ms.
source: Considering that processing times in the retina approach ~50 ms (White et al., 2009), a conservative estimate for the onset of suppression according to the model ranges from 100 ms to 50 ms prior to movement onset.
evidence: This is a quantitative estimate from previous research.

claim: A conservative estimate for the onset of suppression according to the model ranges from 100 ms to 50 ms prior to movement onset.
source: Considering that processing times in the retina approach ~50 ms (White et al., 2009), a conservative estimate for the onset of suppression according to the model ranges from 100 ms to 50 ms prior to movement onset.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the model combined with known retinal processing times.

claim: The presence of a catch up saccade is sufficient to evoke a transient increase in extrapolation variance.
source: The presence of a catch up saccade, even a small one (4deg in Figure 2), is sufficient to evoke a transient increase in extrapolation variance (Figure 2d–f).
evidence: This is shown in the model simulations in Figure 2d-f.

claim: A catch-up saccade results in a reduction in the weight of sensory feedback with similar timing as for larger saccades.
source: This results in a reduction in the weight of sensory feedback with similar timing as for larger saccades.
evidence: This is a model prediction based on the simulation results.

claim: When the eye starts moving smoothly without a catch-up saccade, the model predicts no visible change in the weight of sensory feedback.
source: In contrast, when the eye starts moving smoothly (Figure 2f), there is no catch-up saccade needed and the model predicts no visible change in the weight of sensory feedback.
evidence: This is a model prediction shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Suppression occurs for saccades specifically because of the high control signals required for these movements.
source: The fact that suppression occurs for saccades specifically results from the high control signals required for these movements.
evidence: This is an explanation of model behavior.

claim: The pursuit task without a saccade uses smaller control signals that do not evoke any visible change in the weight of sensory feedback.
source: In contrast, the pursuit task without a saccade uses smaller control signals that do not evoke any visible change in the weight of sensory feedback.
evidence: This is a description of model behavior.

claim: Saccades but not smooth pursuit elicit suppression of sensory feedback.
source: The behavioral finding (Schütz et al., 2007) that saccades but not smooth pursuit elicit suppression of sensory feedback, and that the suppression scales with the amplitude of the catch-up saccade, directly results from this model.
evidence: This is a comparison between model predictions and experimental findings.

claim: Suppression scales with the amplitude of the catch-up saccade.
source: The behavioral finding (Schütz et al., 2007) that saccades but not smooth pursuit elicit suppression of sensory feedback, and that the suppression scales with the amplitude of the catch-up saccade, directly results from this model.
evidence: This is a comparison between model predictions and experimental findings.

claim: Suppression should occur prior to movement onset according to the model.
source: According to our hypothesis, suppression should occur prior to movement onset, reach a maximum close to movement onset (Figure 3b), and scale with the movement amplitude with relatively invariant timing across amplitudes.
evidence: This is a model prediction shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Suppression should reach a maximum close to movement onset.
source: According to our hypothesis, suppression should occur prior to movement onset, reach a maximum close to movement onset (Figure 3b), and scale with the movement amplitude with relatively invariant timing across amplitudes.
evidence: This is a model prediction shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Suppression should scale with the movement amplitude with relatively invariant timing across amplitudes.
source: According to our hypothesis, suppression should occur prior to movement onset, reach a maximum close to movement onset (Figure 3b), and scale with the movement amplitude with relatively invariant timing across amplitudes.
evidence: This is a model prediction shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Microsaccades induce partial suppression despite being very small in amplitude.
source: Interestingly, this goes even down to the level of microsaccades, inducing partial suppression despite being very small in amplitude (Hafed and Krauzlis, 2010).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from previous research.

claim: Contrast sensitivity is reduced during saccades.
source: These known properties of saccadic suppression are in line with the model prediction (Figure 3b, black): contrast sensitivity is reduced and visual stimuli such as flashes, gratings, or small displacements are less likely to be accurately perceived (Diamond et al., 2000; Burr et al., 1994; Watson and Krekelberg, 2011; Burr et al., 1999; Bridgeman et al., 1975; Beeler, 1967).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Visual stimuli such as flashes, gratings, or small displacements are less likely to be accurately perceived during saccades.
source: These known properties of saccadic suppression are in line with the model prediction (Figure 3b, black): contrast sensitivity is reduced and visual stimuli such as flashes, gratings, or small displacements are less likely to be accurately perceived (Diamond et al., 2000; Burr et al., 1994; Watson and Krekelberg, 2011; Burr et al., 1999; Bridgeman et al., 1975; Beeler, 1967).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Suppression occurs even when the stimuli are chosen so that the eye movement does not change the retinal image.
source: This even happens when the stimuli are chosen so that the eye movement does not change the retinal image, which is compatible with the model (see the simulated contrast reduction of a white stripe, Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a comparison between experimental findings and model predictions shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Timing of suppression is preserved across amplitudes.
source: Finally, although timing is preserved across amplitudes (Ibbotson and Krekelberg, 2011), the model predicts that the magnitude of suppression scales with the saccade amplitude as observed experimentally (Ridder and Tomlinson, 1997).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from previous research.

claim: The magnitude of suppression scales with the saccade amplitude.
source: Finally, although timing is preserved across amplitudes (Ibbotson and Krekelberg, 2011), the model predicts that the magnitude of suppression scales with the saccade amplitude as observed experimentally (Ridder and Tomlinson, 1997).
evidence: This is a model prediction that matches experimental findings.

claim: The scaling of suppression magnitude with saccade amplitude is a direct consequence of signal-dependent noise.
source: This scaling is a direct consequence of signal-dependent noise.
evidence: This is an explanation of the model mechanism.

claim: The best explanation for saccadic suppression is a stimulus-independent reduction in the response gain.
source: In addition to capturing the major aspects of behavioral and neural suppression, our model explains the previous findings of Watson and colleagues (Watson and Krekelberg, 2011), who investigated the detection of noisy gratings in humans, and found that the best explanation for saccadic suppression was a stimulus-independent reduction in the response gain.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from previous research.

claim: The retinal images do not become intrinsically noisier during saccades; instead it is the visual system that responds less to a given stimulus.
source: This result is a key aspect of saccadic suppression: the retinal images do not become intrinsically noisier; instead it is the visual system that responds less to a given stimulus.
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental findings.

claim: By reducing the sensory weight in the Kalman gain, the controller becomes less sensitive to sensory information.
source: Our model also accounts for this observation: by reducing the sensory weight in the Kalman gain, the controller becomes less sensitive to sensory information.
evidence: This is an explanation of the model mechanism.

claim: The stimulus-independent reduction in response gain is due to the uncertainty induced by the motor commands.
source: This is due to the uncertainty induced by the motor commands, which is clearly independent of the retinal image.
evidence: This is an explanation of the model mechanism.

claim: The increase in extrapolation variance results from convolving the motor-dependent noise with the expected eye dynamics over the delay interval.
source: First, the increase in extrapolation variance clearly results from convolving the motor-dependent noise with the expected eye dynamics over the delay interval.
evidence: This is an explanation of the mathematical operation in the model.

claim: The increase in extrapolation variance is directly proportional to the integrated motor command.
source: Second, this increase is directly proportional to the integrated motor command.
evidence: This is a mathematical property of the model.

claim: Previous models of saccadic control tend to only consider open-loop controllers or closed-loop control with internal feedback only.
source: While previous models of saccadic control tend to only consider open-loop controllers (Harris and Wolpert, 1998), or closed-loop control with internal feedback only (Optican, 2009; Jürgens et al., 1981; Chen-Harris et al., 2008), there is evidence that sensory information remains available and may influence online control.
evidence: This is a characterization of previous modeling approaches supported by citations.

claim: There is evidence that sensory information remains available and may influence online control during saccades.
source: While previous models of saccadic control tend to only consider open-loop controllers (Harris and Wolpert, 1998), or closed-loop control with internal feedback only (Optican, 2009; Jürgens et al., 1981; Chen-Harris et al., 2008), there is evidence that sensory information remains available and may influence online control.
evidence: This is a general statement about experimental evidence.

claim: Peri-saccadic target jumps evoke adaptation.
source: Indeed, motion detection during saccades is not suppressed (Castet and Masson, 2000), and peri-saccadic target jumps evoke adaptation (Panouillères et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from previous research.

claim: A large retinal slip prior to saccade initiation can elicit curved movements.
source: In addition, a large retinal slip prior to saccade initiation can elicit curved movements (Schreiber et al., 2006), indicating that retinal information prior to saccade onset can influence online control.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from previous research.

claim: Retinal information prior to saccade onset can influence online control.
source: In addition, a large retinal slip prior to saccade initiation can elicit curved movements (Schreiber et al., 2006), indicating that retinal information prior to saccade onset can influence online control.
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental findings.

claim: Gaveau and colleagues reported partial corrections of eye trajectories following target jumps occurring during long saccades.
source: Finally, Gaveau and colleagues reported partial corrections of eye trajectories following target jumps occurring during long saccades (Gaveau et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from previous research.

claim: Partial corrections of target jumps can be explained by lower weight of sensory feedback leading to only partial correction.
source: The fact that these corrections accounted for a small proportion of the target jump can be explained in the model, as a lower weight of sensory feedback leads to only partial correction of the target jump (estimates take longer to converge to the true value).
evidence: This is an explanation of experimental findings using the model.

claim: The model predicts that sensory feedback must be strongly reduced, but not completely suppressed.
source: Based on this assumption, our model predicts that sensory feedback must be strongly reduced, but not completely suppressed, as observed experimentally (Castet and Masson, 2000).
evidence: This is a model prediction that matches experimental findings.

claim: The Kalman filter achieves an optimal projection in the probabilistic sense by making the estimation error orthogonal to the estimated state.
source: This is because the Kalman filter achieves an optimal projection in the probabilistic sense, by making the estimation error orthogonal to (or statistically uncorrelated with) the estimated state.
evidence: This is a property of Kalman filtering theory.

claim: The decrease in the Kalman gain during movement indicates that state information prior to the saccade still carries some information about the current state.
source: Thus, the decrease in the Kalman gain during movement indicates that state information prior to the saccade still carries some information about the current state, and thus can be exploited to derive optimal estimates.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model behavior.

claim: Perception and action share estimates of target speed.
source: There are already strong pieces of evidence for shared resources. Indeed, previous work emphasized that perception and action share estimates of target speed (Priebe and Lisberger, 2004).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from previous research.

claim: A strong link between saccadic suppression and visual-motor neurons has been established in superior colliculus of macaque monkeys.
source: Recently, a strong link between saccadic suppression and visual-motor neurons has been established in superior colliculus of macaque monkeys (Chen and Hafed, 2017).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from previous research.

claim: Perception is conditional upon the ability to integrate extra-retinal signals accurately, both during saccades and pursuit.
source: Furthermore, the motion on its own must not be suppressed to maintain perceptual stability, instead it must be equal to the commanded movement monitored online, thus perception is also conditional upon the ability to integrate extra-retinal signals accurately, both during saccades and pursuit (Sommer and Wurtz, 2008; Blohm et al., 2005; Hafed and Krauzlis, 2010; Bedell and Lott, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: If perceptual and sensorimotor processes were completely decoupled, posterior beliefs about sensory information could be separated from movement-related effects.
source: If perceptual and sensorimotor processes were completely decoupled, posterior beliefs about sensory information could be separated from movement-related effects, and perception around the time of saccades could be as good as during simulated saccades (Figure 4, H1).
evidence: This is a hypothetical scenario presented for comparison.

claim: A motor origin of saccadic suppression implies that the same posterior beliefs are shared for perception and control.
source: Alternatively, a motor origin of saccadic suppression implies that the same posterior beliefs are shared for perception and control, which is suboptimal as it impacts perception of otherwise reliable sensory signals (Figure 4, H2).
evidence: This is the hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: The shared resources model is cheaper in terms of neural resources.
source: Although perception on its own is suboptimal during saccades (we discard a lot of meaningful information), the shared resources model is clearly cheaper in terms of neural resources.
evidence: This is a logical inference about resource efficiency.

claim: It may be globally optimal to tolerate perceptual loss during saccades rather than commit to more neural resources for visual processing.
source: It may thus be globally optimal to tolerate perceptual loss during saccades rather than commit to more neural resources for visual processing, considering perceptual and control systems together.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the shared resources hypothesis.

claim: Using the same posterior belief for perception and action ensures self-consistency.
source: Using the same posterior belief for perception and action also ensures self-consistency, in the sense that the same stimulus is not deemed more or less reliable dependent on how we use it.
evidence: This is a logical argument for the shared resources hypothesis.

claim: Self-consistency characterizes perceptual judgment tasks, where participants make continuous use of the hypothesis to which they previously committed.
source: Self-consistency is known to characterize perceptual judgment tasks, where participants make continuous use of the hypothesis to which they previously committed (Stocker and Simoncelli, 2007).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from previous research.

claim: There is neural suppression across the hierarchy of visual areas during saccades.
source: Indeed, a large number of experimental studies have found such a neural suppression across the hierarchy of visual areas. (Ibbotson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Neural suppression occurs in the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) during saccades.
source: The pathways begin with the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) (Reppas et al., 2002) and the superior colliculus (SC) (Hafed and Krauzlis, 2010), and continue in the cortical areas V1 (Kagan et al., 2008), MT, MST, MSTd (Ibbotson et al., 2008; Bremmer et al., 2009), and VIP (Bremmer et al., 2009) (Figure 3b, colored bars).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Neural suppression occurs in the superior colliculus (SC) during saccades.
source: The pathways begin with the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) (Reppas et al., 2002) and the superior colliculus (SC) (Hafed and Krauzlis, 2010), and continue in the cortical areas V1 (Kagan et al., 2008), MT, MST, MSTd (Ibbotson et al., 2008; Bremmer et al., 2009), and VIP (Bremmer et al., 2009) (Figure 3b, colored bars).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Neural suppression occurs in cortical area V1 during saccades.
source: The pathways begin with the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) (Reppas et al., 2002) and the superior colliculus (SC) (Hafed and Krauzlis, 2010), and continue in the cortical areas V1 (Kagan et al., 2008), MT, MST, MSTd (Ibbotson et al., 2008; Bremmer et al., 2009), and VIP (Bremmer et al., 2009) (Figure 3b, colored bars).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Neural suppression occurs in cortical areas MT, MST, and MSTd during saccades.
source: The pathways begin with the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) (Reppas et al., 2002) and the superior colliculus (SC) (Hafed and Krauzlis, 2010), and continue in the cortical areas V1 (Kagan et al., 2008), MT, MST, MSTd (Ibbotson et al., 2008; Bremmer et al., 2009), and VIP (Bremmer et al., 2009) (Figure 3b, colored bars).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Neural suppression occurs in cortical area VIP during saccades.
source: The pathways begin with the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) (Reppas et al., 2002) and the superior colliculus (SC) (Hafed and Krauzlis, 2010), and continue in the cortical areas V1 (Kagan et al., 2008), MT, MST, MSTd (Ibbotson et al., 2008; Bremmer et al., 2009), and VIP (Bremmer et al., 2009) (Figure 3b, colored bars).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The timing of neural suppression is very similar across brain regions.
source: Interestingly, the timing is very similar across brain regions, which emerges naturally from the fact that the loop through the outside world with its delays is the dominating timescale.
evidence: This is an observation about the consistency of neural suppression timing with an explanation.

claim: Cancelling the retinal shift induced by the saccade does not explain the phenomenon of saccadic suppression.
source: The important motivation behind this study was that cancelling the retinal shift induced by the saccade, as commonly assumed, does not explain the phenomenon of saccadic suppression.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of previous explanations.

claim: If suppression were only for cancelling retinal shift, it should only occur when the eyes move and should not be stronger than the moderate loss in performance associated with simulated saccades.
source: Indeed, suppression in this case should only occur when the eyes move, and should not be stronger than the moderate loss in performance associated with saccades simulated as a rapid displacement of the visual scene (Diamond et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a logical argument against the retinal shift cancellation hypothesis.

claim: If saccadic suppression were purely for maintaining perceptual stability, all discarded information beyond movement-related effects would represent a net loss.
source: All discarded information beyond movement-related effects would otherwise represent a net loss (up to ~100 ms for some brain areas, Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a logical argument about the inefficiency of suppression if it were only for perceptual stability.

claim: If it were possible to train participants to pay attention to visual stimuli displayed during saccades, the theory predicts that movement trajectories should become more variable.
source: That is, if it were possible to train participants to pay attention to visual stimuli displayed during saccades, thereby increasing the weight of sensory feedback, then the theory predicts that movement trajectories should become more variable as a result of suboptimal state estimation.
evidence: This is a testable prediction derived from the model.

claim: The locus of attention and the goal of saccadic movements are linked.
source: There is already clear evidence that the locus of attention and the goal of saccadic movements are linked (Kowler et al., 1995) (and many references thereto).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Saccade trajectories should become more variable from trial to trial when participants are forced to use sensory information presented during the interval of saccadic suppression.
source: Here our specific prediction is that saccade trajectories should become more variable from trial to trial when participants are forced to use sensory information presented during the interval of saccadic suppression.
evidence: This is a specific testable prediction from the model.

claim: Varying the reliability of sensory information may have an impact on the magnitude of saccadic suppression.
